items.title: Hermes Agent v0.21.6
items.content:
Hermes Agent v0.21.6
Release Date: October 8, 2026

Patch release. This tag rolls up the ~2,100 PRs merged since v0.21.5 into a stable tagged release for Docker and Hermes Cloud. Full curated notes for this window ship with v0.22.0.


About this release
This is the first release cut by the new stable release pipeline: one attempt ref, a tested Docker image, and a receipt tag at publish. It ships the tag, this GitHub release and the Docker image. The desktop app, Termux packages and the Microsoft Store stay on their current build for now and move with the next bundled release.
Measured at commit 818c13be1dc4fd28987e1e881a9408224afd4535, the window since v0.21.5 contains 8,867 non-merge commits across 8,342 changed files (+772,490 / −225,600), 2,106 merged PRs and 3,027 closed issues.
Also in the window, undocumented here on purpose: live transcription while you speak on CLI, TUI and Desktop (stt.streaming); spoken voice turns routed to their own model (auxiliary.voice_chat) with reasoning off by default; third-party plugins running in a per-profile plugin host (plugins.isolation: host) and one Settings ▸ Plugins home for their settings pages; favorite and pinned models at the top of the Desktop picker, a usage chip before a subscription hits its wall, and rate-limited providers that say why and until when; local models in hermes model plus llama.cpp CUDA on Linux x64 and arm64; pluggable, layered language packs across core, Desktop and TUI; a summary-first hermes status (--short, --full); a review-pane diff scope selector (Uncommitted / Branch / Last turn) and keep-awake that follows the turn; cron, doctor and home-channel warnings when the cron store goes unwritable; approval flags for credential uploads and invisible Unicode in terminal commands; a Discord setup that checks the bot token and prints the invite link; a unified Kanban workflow definition; activate.fish; GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5 / Haiku 5.5 in the catalogs; and dozens of new community plugins.
Full curated release notes for this window ship with v0.22.0, which will document everything from v0.21.0 onward — highlights, feature areas, and complete contributor credits. Nothing in this window is skipped.
Updating

Docker / Hermes Cloud: nousresearch/hermes-agent:stable (or :latest).
CLI (git installs): hermes update, or re-run the installer one-liner.
Desktop app and Termux: no change in this release; they update with the next bundled release.

Security Fixes
Dashboard authentication hardening

Spoofed X-Forwarded-For headers could reset the password-login rate limit and get around the per-IP cap on native sign-in (#133367)
Unauthenticated login requests could write unbounded values to the auth audit log (#133369)
The public /auth/ routes had no request-body size limit (#133370)
Native sign-in could send login codes to a non-loopback redirect, which allowed session takeover (#130685)

Thanks to Tenable Research for reporting all four issues (TRA-725, TRA-726, TRA-727, TRA-728). The native sign-in redirect issue was also reported independently and fixed by @Froraut. The X-Forwarded-For fix builds on community work by @Hinotoi-agent and @BearHuddleston (#40285).
Repository git filter hardening

Automatic git calls (session workspace snapshot, subagent worktrees, kanban, worktree cleanup, hermes -w) could run clean/smudge/process filter programs defined by an untrusted repository's own config, before the first prompt (#130661)

Thanks to 燕涛 for reporting this privately. It was also reported and fixed publicly by @jonpol01 (#126017, #126019) and @JoaoMarcos44 (#126075).
Email gateway sender hardening

A quoted display name in the From header (e.g. "Victim <victim@example.com>" <attacker@evil.test>) could make an attacker's message pass the email allowlist as an allowed sender (#125212)

Thanks to Daniel Steele (@keeltrace) for reporting this and writing the fix (#124322).
Full Changelog: v2026.9.24...v0.21.6

items.title: Herald OS: The Free Hermes Agent Operating System, Tested
items.content:
Herald OS is a free, open-source, agent-native operating system with Hermes Agent as the interface — and honestly, it’s the best-looking way to use Hermes I’ve seen. You talk or type to Hermes, and it works across your whole machine. I set it up and gave you the full tour in the video below. Here’s what it does, how to get it, and how it compares with Hermes Desktop.

Key takeaways

Herald OS is free and MIT-licensed, built by independent developer Luke The Dev.
It wraps Hermes Agent in a full OS-style interface: dashboard, spaces, missions, memory, files and automations.
It runs as a Mac app (Apple Silicon) or a full Linux system.
It’s early alpha — brilliant design, a few rough edges.






What Herald OS is
Herald OS describes itself as an agent-native operating system with Hermes Agent as the interface. Instead of opening apps and clicking around yourself, you tell Hermes what you want — open an app, sort your files, run a routine — and it does it, asking permission before it changes anything.
It’s built by Luke The Dev, who posts loads of Hermes content on X. Shout out to Luke — this is a seriously impressive project. It’s independent, not made by Nous Research, but it runs on Hermes Agent, which is installed alongside it.




Herald OS at a glance





What it is
An agent-native operating system with Hermes Agent as the interface


Made by
Luke The Dev (iamlukethedev) — independent, not affiliated with Nous Research


Price
Free — MIT licence; you only pay for the AI model you connect


Version
0.1 alpha — early software


Platforms
macOS app (Apple Silicon, macOS 13+), Herald OS Linux (Fedora-based ISO), Arch/Omarchy package, Linux tarball


Needs
Hermes Agent, plus a Nous Portal account or an API key for a supported provider


Source
github.com/iamlukethedev/Herald-OS




How I set up Herald OS
I literally opened Claude and said, “Can you set this up?” About two minutes later, Herald OS was running. If you’d rather do it yourself, the steps for every platform are in my Herald OS GitHub install guide.
Why bother with an operating system for your agent? Because it makes Hermes far easier to navigate and command. When Hermes first came out, back around March or April, we all ran it in the terminal and it was messy. A proper interface changes how much you actually use it.

Want this working in your business, not just bookmarked? Setting up an agent operating system for your business is exactly what we build together inside the AI Profit Boardroom — 3,400+ members, four live calls a week, and a full one-hour DeepSeek Harness course in the classroom.
Prefer it mapped 1-on-1 first? Book a free strategy session and we’ll plan it for your exact situation.

Join the AI Profit Boardroom →Book a Free Strategy Session →

A tour of the Herald OS dashboard
When you open it, it says “Good morning, Julian — your day already in motion.” It pulls in your scheduled tasks for the day, shows what needs attention, and suggests where to pick up where you left off, based on your recent documents, projects, chats and calendar events. You can switch that on or off. You can talk to it with your voice, and it even used screenshots I’d recently taken on my desktop to show what I’ve been working on.




Section
What it does




Overview
Your day at a glance: scheduled tasks, what needs attention, and up to three “pick up where you left off” suggestions


Hermes
Chat with Hermes normally, with a preview pane and sources Hermes can read


Spaces
Separate Ideas, Work and Personal spaces — add more for clients or companies


Missions
Give Hermes a goal and it plans it out step by step


Memory
See and manage everything Hermes remembers about you


Files
Recent, favourites, projects, downloads, shared and deleted files Hermes can access


Automations
Switch scheduled routines on and off


Connections
Bring apps and tools into your agents


Settings
Models, where agents run (including Docker), background agents, approvals, history, themes, plugins, voice and privacy




Herald OS spaces and missions
Spaces are one of my favourite features. You get Ideas, Work and Personal out of the box, and you can add more. Inside the AI Profit Boardroom I constantly get the question: “If I have separate companies or clients, how should I set up my agent OS?” This is a really clean answer — one space per client or company.
Missions are where you give Hermes a bigger goal — “build out a new website for me” — and it plans the work out step by step and gets going.
Herald OS settings worth knowing

Preferred model — I had GPT-6 Astra running through its CLI.
Where agents run — including Docker, which a lot of people ask about.
Background agents — how many can run at once.
Approvals — auto-approve on or off, and ask before sending messages.
Activity history — see everything Hermes has done.
General — full screen, default space, projects folder, do not disturb, stay awake, screen saver, dictation.
Themes — twelve built in, and you can make your own.
Software — manage coding agents and local models like Claude Code, Codex and LM Studio.
Plugins — paste a GitHub link and click add.
Usage — tokens used, plan and balance.
Voice — choose a local or live engine and see all the voice commands.

Herald OS vs Hermes Desktop




Option
What it is
Best for




Herald OS
A full, free agent-native OS UI around Hermes — open source, alpha
People who want the nicest-looking Hermes interface and don’t mind early software


Hermes Desktop
Nous Research’s official Hermes app, with a plugin catalogue
Stability and official support


My Agent OS (AI Profit Boardroom)
My agentic operating system — manages Hermes and other agents in one place
Running several agents, not just Hermes, with training and support


Hermes in the terminal
The original way to run Hermes
Developers who live in the command line




Here’s the cool part: my automations synced across Herald OS, Hermes Desktop and my Agent OS — my daily 6am to-do recap, daily Japanese practice and morning inbox triage showed up in all three. So you don’t have to pick just one. Hermes Desktop has the official plugin marketplace; Herald OS has the nicer design.
Herald OS: what to watch out for

It’s alpha software — expect rough edges. In my test the top of the window cut off slightly and Connections didn’t sync for me.
The Mac app isn’t notarised by Apple yet, which is why the setup removes the quarantine flag — only do that for a build you downloaded from the official releases page.
Check what’s on screen before you share it — the Memory page showed my Telegram details while I was recording.
Keep approvals on — leave “ask before sending messages” switched on until you trust your setup.
Review the activity history — Hermes can set things up in the background that you forget about.

My verdict on Herald OS
Herald OS is super clean, easy to use and synced up quickly. If you want a beautiful interface for Hermes and you don’t love Hermes Desktop, it’s a great free option — just remember it’s alpha, and expect to fix the odd thing along the way.
FAQ: herald os
Is Herald OS free?
Yes — it’s free and open source under the MIT licence. You only pay for the AI model you connect to Hermes.
Is Herald OS made by Nous Research?
No — it’s an independent project by Luke The Dev. It runs on Hermes Agent, which is made by Nous Research.
What is Herald OS?
An agent-native operating system with Hermes Agent as the interface — you talk or type to Hermes and it works across your machine.
What platforms does Herald OS run on?
A Mac app for Apple Silicon (macOS 13+), a Fedora-based Herald OS Linux ISO, an Arch/Omarchy package and a Linux tarball.
Is Herald OS better than Hermes Desktop?
It looks nicer and organises work into spaces and missions; Hermes Desktop is official and more stable. Your automations can sync across both.
Is Herald OS safe?
It asks before changing anything and logs actions, but it’s alpha software — keep approvals on and check the activity history.

Or grab a free strategy session and bring your questions.

items.title: Hermes Agent OS GitHub: Install Herald OS on Mac or Linux
items.content:
The Hermes Agent OS GitHub repo you want is iamlukethedev/Herald-OS — the free, open-source operating system with Hermes Agent as the interface. In the video below I show it running. This guide gives you the exact install commands for every platform, the requirements, and the gotchas to watch for.

Key takeaways

The repo is github.com/iamlukethedev/Herald-OS (MIT licence).
Mac: install Hermes, run hermes setup, then install the DMG from Releases.
Linux: a Fedora-based ISO, an Arch package or a tarball.
It’s 0.1 alpha — read the open issues first.






The Hermes Agent OS GitHub repository

entry, existing installs keep working. Author notified:

items.title: Hermes Herald AI Agent: How Hermes Runs Your Whole Computer in Herald OS
items.content:
The Hermes Herald AI agent is Hermes Agent running as the interface to Herald OS — a free, open-source operating system where you talk or type to Hermes and it works across your whole computer. In the video below I show it in action. This guide focuses on the agent side: what Hermes can do inside Herald, how it asks permission, and how to command it well.

Key takeaways

In Herald OS, Hermes Agent is the interface — it opens apps, organises files and runs routines for you.
Every system tool has a permission tier; anything that changes or deletes things asks first.
Talk to it with push-to-talk or “hey Hermes”.
Not to be confused with Hermes v0.20 “Herald”, the earlier Hermes release.






What the Hermes Herald AI agent is
Herald OS is an independent project by Luke The Dev that puts Hermes Agent at the centre of your computer. You don’t open apps and click through menus — you tell Hermes what you need, and it does the work across the machine.
Quick clarification, because the names overlap: “Herald” was also the codename of the Hermes v0.20 release back in August, which added voice and agent-to-agent features. I covered that in my Hermes Herald release guide. This page is about Hermes as the agent inside Herald OS.
How the Hermes Herald AI agent controls your computer
Herald OS connects to Hermes through a plugin called herald-os-bridge, which gives Hermes a set of system tools. Each tool has a permission tier:




Tool tier
What happens




Read
Runs directly and is logged


Act
Runs directly and is logged


Mutate
Asks you first


Destructive
Asks you every single time




Every action is written to an audit log, so you can always see what your agent did. The developer has also tightened things so Herald’s system tools only run inside Herald OS sessions — not in your other Hermes sessions like messaging or cron jobs.

Want this working in your business, not just bookmarked? Running Hermes Agent as your AI employee is exactly what we build together inside the AI Profit Boardroom — 3,400+ members, four live calls a week, and a full one-hour DeepSeek Harness course in the classroom.
Prefer it mapped 1-on-1 first? Book a free strategy session and we’ll plan it for your exact situation.

Join the AI Profit Boardroom →Book a Free Strategy Session →

Giving the Hermes Herald AI agent missions
Missions are for bigger goals. Type something like “build out a new website for me” and Hermes plans it out step by step, then starts working. There’s also a Studio feature that builds a project from a description with a live preview.
For day-to-day work, the dashboard does the thinking for you: it looks at your recent files, projects, chats and calendar and suggests up to three threads to pick back up. And if an app crashes, Hermes can explain the crash report in plain English.
Talking to Hermes in Herald OS
Voice is one of the most useful parts. Use a push-to-talk key or say “hey Hermes”, and choose between a free voice engine and an opt-in real-time one. It feels like having Jarvis on your computer. There’s a full list of voice commands in Settings, and the latest update lets you find, read, name and file documents by voice — perfect for sorting a folder of badly named PDFs.
Memory, files and spaces

Memory — see everything Hermes remembers about you, and manage it.
Files — control exactly which files Hermes can access.
Spaces — keep Ideas, Work and Personal separate, and add spaces for each client or company.
Automations — your scheduled routines, switched on and off in one place, synced with Hermes Desktop.


Careful when you screen-share: my Memory page showed my Telegram details while recording. Check what’s visible before you share your screen.

Setting up the Hermes Herald AI agent safely

Start with auto-approve off and “ask before sending messages” on.
Limit background agents until you know what’s running.
Check the activity history regularly — it’s easy to forget what you set up.
Give Hermes access to the folders it needs, not your whole drive.
Remember it’s alpha software — keep backups of anything important.

For the full install steps, see my Herald OS GitHub guide, and for the overall tour, my Herald OS review.
Hermes Herald AI agent vs Hermes Desktop





Hermes in Herald OS
Hermes Desktop




Made by
Luke The Dev (independent)
Nous Research (official)


Scope
Runs your whole computer — apps, files, system settings
An app for chatting with and configuring Hermes


Organisation
Spaces, missions, a daily dashboard
Profiles, chats, plugin catalogue


Voice
Push-to-talk, “hey Hermes”, free or real-time engine
Via voice plugins


Maturity
0.1 alpha
Stable releases




The big difference is scope. Hermes Desktop is where you talk to your agent; in Herald OS, Hermes is the computer’s front door. You can run both — my automations showed up in each.
Example commands to try

“Prep my day” — check my calendar and what’s scheduled, then tell me what needs attention.
“Sort my Downloads folder and rename the PDFs properly.”
“Set up a daily 6am to-do recap.”
“Start a mission: build a landing page for my new offer.”
“Explain why that app just crashed.”
“Switch to my Work space and open my latest project.”

Start with read-only requests while you learn how it behaves, then move on to ones that change things once you’re comfortable with the approval prompts.
Is the Hermes Herald AI agent worth it?
If you already use Hermes, this is the most natural way I’ve seen to let it run your computer: clean design, sensible permissions and voice built in. The Hermes Herald AI agent setup is free — try it, keep approvals on, and build from there.
One last tip: treat Hermes in Herald OS like a new team member. Give it small, clear jobs first, check its work in the activity history, and widen its permissions only as it earns your trust. That approach has worked for every agent I’ve set up, and it’s the fastest way to get real value without nasty surprises.
FAQ: hermes herald ai agent
Is Herald OS free?
Yes — it’s free and open source under the MIT licence. You only pay for the AI model you connect to Hermes.
Is Herald OS made by Nous Research?
No — it’s an independent project by Luke The Dev. It runs on Hermes Agent, which is made by Nous Research.
What is the Hermes Herald AI agent?
Hermes Agent running as the interface to Herald OS, where it opens apps, organises files and runs routines across your computer.
Is it the same as the Hermes Herald release?
No — “Herald” was also the codename for Hermes v0.20 in August 2026. Herald OS is a separate, independent operating system built on Hermes.
Does Hermes ask before changing things in Herald OS?
Yes — tools that change things ask first, destructive tools ask every time, and everything is logged.
Can I talk to Hermes in Herald OS?
Yes — with a push-to-talk key or the “hey Hermes” wake phrase.

Remember it’s alpha software — keep backups of anything important.

The big difference is scope. Hermes Desktop is where you talk to your agent; in Herald OS, Hermes is the computer’s front door. You can run both — my automations showed up in each.

“Prep my day” — check my calendar and what’s scheduled, then tell me what needs attention.

Start with read-only requests while you learn how it behaves, then move on to ones that change things once you’re comfortable with the approval prompts.

Is the Hermes Herald AI agent worth it?

If you already use Hermes, this is the most natural way I’ve seen to let it run your computer: clean design, sensible permissions and voice built in. The Hermes Herald AI agent setup is free — try it, keep approvals on, and build from there.

One last tip: treat Hermes in Herald OS like a new team member. Give it small, clear jobs first, check its work in the activity history, and widen its permissions only as it earns your trust. That approach has worked for every agent I’ve set up, and it’s the fastest way to get real value without nasty surprises.

FAQ: hermes herald ai agent

Is Herald OS free?

Yes — it’s free and open source under the MIT licence. You only pay for the AI model you connect to Hermes.

Is Herald OS made by Nous Research?

No — it’s an independent project by Luke The Dev. It runs on Hermes Agent, which is made by Nous Research.

What is the Hermes Herald AI agent?

Hermes Agent running as the interface to Herald OS, where it opens apps, organises files and runs routines across your computer.

Is it the same as the Hermes Herald release?

No — “Herald” was also the codename for Hermes v0.20 in August 2026. Herald OS is a separate, independent operating system built on Hermes.

Does Hermes ask before changing things in Herald OS?

Yes — tools that change things ask first, destructive tools ask every time, and everything is logged.

Can I talk to Hermes in Herald OS?

Yes — with a push-to-talk key or the “hey Hermes” wake phrase.

items.content:
test(desktop): the React Compiler cache is its own module with focused tests

The cache lived inline in vite.config.ts, and the renderer builder tests use a bare fixture
config, so nothing exercised it: a broken warm path would still pass every test.

Move it to scripts/compiler-cache.mjs (behaviour unchanged; toolchain files and cache root are
now parameters, and an existing closeBundle hook is chained instead of replaced) and test hit
vs fresh output, toolchain/NODE_ENV generations, corrupt entries, pruning, incremental (watch)
rebuilds and the dev-server bypass. A cold and warm production build of the real app stay
byte-identical. Reported by Greptile on #135092.

items.title: test(desktop): model settings tests clear their toast timers before j…
items.content:
test(desktop): model settings tests clear their toast timers before jsdom tears down

The main-model apply test raises a success toast, which arms a 5 s
auto-dismiss timer. Nothing cleared it, so when it fired after the file's
jsdom window was gone, vitest reported "window is not defined" from
dismissNotification as an unhandled error and failed JS & TS checks with
every test green. afterEach now calls clearNotifications().
items.author: teknium1
items.summary: A desktop test fix ensures model settings tests clear their toast auto-dismiss timers before jsdom teardown, resolving failures where vitest reported window is not defined from dismissNotification even with all tests green. The afterEach hook now calls clearNotifications.
items.reasoning: This is an internal test-infrastructure fix for the Hermes Desktop codebase with no direct user-facing behavior change. It improves CI reliability for contributors, but most Hermes users will be unaffected.
items.summary_html: A desktop test fix ensures model settings tests clear their toast auto-dismiss timers before jsdom teardown, resolving failures where vitest reported window is not defined from dismissNotification even with all tests green. The afterEach hook now calls clearNotifications.
